title: Gears of War: E-Day incelemeleri yayınlandı
summary: The Coalition tarafından geliştirilen Gears of War: E-Day, serinin köklerine dönerken aksiyon odaklı yapısıyla 6 Ekim'de çıkıyor.
body:
Gears of War: E-Day incelemeleri yayınlandı ve The Coalition tarafından geliştirilen yeni yapım, Xbox'ın en önemli serilerinden birini köklerine döndürüyor. İlk oyunun 14 yıl öncesinde geçen bu prequel (önceki dönemi anlatan) oyun, Locust Horde sürpriziyle yer altından gelen saldırıya karşı hayatta kalmaya çalışan Marcus Fenix ve Dominic Santiago'nun hikayesini konu alıyor. VGC, Polygon ve The Verge gibi teknoloji ve oyun basınının aktardığına göre, oyun serinin klasik siper alıp çatışma mekaniklerini korurken oyunculara zıplama ve kayma gibi yeni hareket özgürlükleri de sunuyor.

## Oynanış ve hikaye eleştirileri

Oyun genel olarak aksiyon dolu temposuyla beğenilse de, bazı incelemelerde yapısal ve hikayesel açıdan eleştiriler de yer alıyor. VGC ve Polygon'un aktardığına göre, oyunun içerisine serpiştirilmiş yarı açık dünya bölümleri ve tekrara düşen bazı mekanlar temposu yüksek olan kampanyayı yer yer zayıflatabiliyor. Karakter ilişkilerinin beklendiği kadar derin işlenmediği belirtilirken, bunun yerine aksiyon odaklı ve klişe film diyaloglarının ön planda olduğu ifade ediliyor. Buna karşın, oynanış hissinin ve grafik detaylarının son derece tatmin edici olduğu vurgulanıyor.

## Çıkış tarihi ve platformlar

Xbox ve Windows PC platformları için geliştirilen yapım, VGC, Polygon ve The Verge kaynaklarına göre 6 Ekim tarihinde oyuncularla buluşuyor. The Coalition imzasını taşıyan oyun, Xbox'ın çalkantılı bir dönemden geçtiği bu günlerde Microsoft platformlarına özel olarak sunulan büyük bir yapım olarak öne çıkıyor.

**Neden önemli?** Xbox serisinin geleceği açısından kritik bir dönemde gelen Gears of War: E-Day, seriyi modern dönem trendlerinden ziyade saf aksiyon köklerine bağlayan ve yalnızca Microsoft platformlarında boy gösteren büyük bütçeli bir yapım olmasıyla dikkat çekiyor.

source_texts.title: Gears of War E-Day campaign review: An absolute blast, even if it focuses on commotion over emotion
source_texts.summary: The Coalition's latest falls short with the story, but delivers great action by the (gun) barrel load
source_texts.text:
There are some series that thrive on innovation, and some that are at their best when they stick to what works. Gears of War very much sits in the latter camp.
Xboxâs action series has never really dipped to the point where itâs ever had a truly bad game, but on the rare occasions where players have pointed out things they werenât so sure about, itâs been when the game strayed away from the tried-and-tested formula.
One of the most notable examples of this is Gears 5âs open-world sections, where players drive through large expanses in the Skiff, a sort of wind-powered sled. While some liked the change of pace, others found these open areas lacking in content, and felt they distracted too much from the more linear combat Gears is usually known for.
With Gears of War: E-Day, developer The Coalition is mostly trying to bring things back to basics. While it does still try to tinker with the formula to some extent â there are still open-world sections, but theyâre not as extreme, which Iâll get to â the majority of the game sticks to the classic Gears action fans of the series expect.
As the name suggests, E-Day is a prequel which takes place 14 years before the events of the first game. It shows what happened during Emergence Day â when the Locust Horde first attacked from under the ground â and how the recently demobilised Marcus and Dom, home after the end of the Pendulum Wars, cope with the new threat.
On paper, thereâs more to it than that. As has already been revealed in previous Gears games, Domâs brother (and Marcusâs best friend) Carlos died right as the Pendulum Wars ended, and because this is a recent event in this game â rather than something that happened a decade and a half ago â Dom and Marcus are still coming to terms with their loss.
Xbox previously hinted that the game would show Marcus and Dom being emotionally distant from each other due to Carlosâs death, and that the Emergence would force them to reluctantly team up again.
In my brief hands-on with the game last month I wrote: âAs much as Gears of War: E-Day is going to be about the arrival of the Locust, itâs also going to be about how these two emotionally distant soldiers, joined by grief for the same person but also kept apart by it, will eventually form the bond we see in later games.â
In practice, that doesnât really come to fruition much. The relationship with Marcus and Dom really doesnât get explored much throughout the majority of the game, and thereâs only really one scene in the final act â and itâs not about Carlos â which really delivers a solid payoff.
In fact, most of the character development is instead focused on the two new characters in the four-person Bravo Team you control throughout the game. Joining Marcus and Dom â purely because they were nearby when the Locust first attacks â are rookie COG cadet Lucas Reyes and 15-year COG veteran Mags Carter, who was dishonorably discharged but finds herself reluctantly picking up a gun again to do her duty when the attack comes.
Itâs Lucas and Mags who have the more interesting backstories, both of which actually lead to some of the locations you visit in the game. Marcus and Dom instead spend most of the game putting off sharing their feelings, which is understandable from a character development point of view but a tad underwhelming from the view of a long-time fan who wants to see them interacting with each other more.
Indeed, the plot is generally the weakest part of E-Day, which is particularly disappointing given itâs literally named after a key plot point. A lot of the first half is basically âwhat are these thingsâ, and the rest is rammed with clichÃ©s and action movie tropes â I shook my head when one NPC actually said, âtell my family I love themâ.
“A lot of the first half is basically ‘what are these things’, and the rest is rammed with clichÃ©s and action movie tropes â I shook my head when one NPC actually said ‘tell my family I love them’.”
Of course, action movie tropes do make sense when what you have here is basically a 10-15 hour action movie anyway. As with the other Gears games, this is a mix of Rambo, Starship Troopers and Predator, with the attention focused squarely on emptying endless rounds of bullets into big ugly alien faces the vast majority of the time.
In that respect, E-Day is a success. The classic cover shooter gameplay of past Gears games returns here, but adds new tweaks to give the player more flexibility. Now you can jump whenever you like, meaning you can climb up surfaces (adding more verticality to some gunfights) or leap across gaps.
You can also now slide across the floor while running, and lie down to take cover behind lower shelter. Obviously, there are numerous action games (especially FPS titles) that have been doing this for years, so itâs not as if E-Day is breaking new ground in the grand scheme of things by adding these features, but it does have a brilliant impact on how the combat feels â moving around from position to position during gunfights feels a lot more dynamic and less like trying to move a truck around.
Gunplay is also still deeply satisfying, which is a good job because itâs what you do 90% of the time. Using your Prototype Lancer to take out the legs of a charging Locust grunt is a treat, and using your Longshot to pop enemy heads from across the length of the battlefield is as gratifying late in Act 5 as it was early in Act 1.
Thereâs a decent variety of enemy types too, from returning baddies to newcomers like the Bilefrog (which can be killed quickly by tossing a frag grenade into its mouth) or the massive Flayer, who uses his Gorehook grapple weapon to pierce your skin from a distance. The optimal way to kill each one is varied enough that when you find yourself in a big stand-off with a bunch of different enemies, it becomes a brilliantly gory ballet of machine guns, exploding heads, chainsaws, and grenades.
As brilliant as the combat is, thereâs no escaping that it leads to a bit of a one-trick pony situation. Dispatching enemies may remain satisfying right up until the final kill that rolls the credits, but it would be a lie to say it didnât feel repetitive during some stretches of the game. There are moments where it does feel like youâre just running from one open area full of things to hide behind, to the next one, to the next.
“Using your Longshot to pop enemy heads from across the length of the battlefield is as gratifying late in Act 5 as it was early in Act 1.”
It also certainly doesn’t help that one location, a large bridge section, is visited on three separate occasions throughout the game, and each time the story involves getting to the control room and either raising or lowering it. By the time you find yourself doing it for the third time, the âfool me onceâ rule comes into effect, and you start wondering if the game is just recycling the same location and set-piece to extend the length of the campaign.

source_texts.title: Gears of War: E-Day Is Gears at Its Finest, Despite One Huge Flaw | Review
source_texts.summary: The Gears of War: E-Day campaign is one of the series' very best, telling the story of where it all began, but the open-world sections are a disappoin
source_texts.text:
Gears of War: E-Day is absolutely relentless. Set during Emergence Day, the name given to the moment the Locust Horde invaded the planet Sera (referenced repeatedly in previous games), this is a prequel to everything we know about Gears of War. For the entire duration of its 20+-hour runtime, you hardly have a moment to breathe.
Taking place across three in-game days, E-Day gives you control of whichever member of Bravo squad takes your fancy: squad leader Marcus Fenix, the iconic Dominic Santiago, cadet Lucas Reyes, or thought-she'd-retired Mags Carter. The four are tasked with repelling the Locust army in any way possible, rescuing survivors, and helping what remains of civilization get back on its feet.
As you'd expect when defending against a surprise invasion by a species you didn't even know existed that threatens all of humanity, Gears of War: E-Day is frantic. The sheer number of enemies means the city of Kalona is rapidly consumed, and when you're done with one combat encounter, the next is merely seconds away. While combat is as strong as it's ever been in the series, this constant barrage means this is unlikely to be a campaign you'll blitz through in a couple of sittings. It's intense, and after a while, exhausting.
Gears of War is back — bolder, bigger, and in many ways better
Structurally, it also takes a huge risk. Sprinkled throughout the linear missions are semi-open-world sections with side objectives and collectibles marked on the in-game map. This isn't the first Gears of War game to implement a non-linear structure — Gears 5 did it with its snowy tundra and red desert sections, but where they were desolate and consisted of going from one landmark to the next, E-Day's open sections are environmentally dense, with alleyways and city streets housing dynamic encounters.
For example, at one point, I stumbled upon a civilian taking cover on a balcony. "Get back," she yelled. "If they spot movement, they'll shoot!" A moment later, I saw the glint of a Locust sniper across the street, and a second later, the civilian's head was blown off. I was too slow to protect her, but had I been a little faster on the trigger, I suspect Fenix could've radioed back to base and gotten a squad of Gears to come and rescue her.
The first of these open-world sections comes a little way into the game's second act of five, and it's perhaps the biggest pace-breaker — to the point where it's far too big. Gears of War: E-Day spends its time stressing how chaotic and urgent everything is, but you're then afforded as much time as you like to wander the city streets, killing seemingly endless Locusts and searching for random collectibles. It's a slog, and there are three more of these open-world interludes still to come.
As is always the case with Gears of War, E-Day excels in its set-pieces and cinematic moments. Defending your airborne raven helicopter against an army of reavers in the middle of a storm feels badass. Taking down one of the game's self-dubbed testicle monsters with a quick bolt-action rifle shot to the eye is satisfying as hell. Shooting endless bullets at a Corpser (an enormous spider-like monster) that has boarded your moving train, before it gets obliterated into smithereens after colliding with the entrance to a bridge, is as gory and epic as you can imagine.
In cutscenes, it's also one of the most jaw-dropping games I've ever played. E-Day loves a close-up of Bravo squad's faces, and for good reason: the visual fidelity is astounding. Still screenshots don't quite do it justice, but in motion, it's beautiful. If you're playing on Windows PC, however, that means you also need a rig to handle it. Despite my PC meeting the recommended specs, finding the balance between a playable frame rate and a satisfactory visual standard was a constant battle.
My experience of E-Day also wasn't without its fair share of bugs (and not of the Locust variety). I encountered a levitating Gear, enemies with questionable pathfinding that saw them running headfirst into a wall over and over, and a number of hitbox issues where bullets wouldn't connect with enemies despite the crosshair turning red and neither of us being in cover, which was the most frustrating of the bunch. At one point, a cutscene triggered before the preceding firefight had ended, resulting in a moment that should’ve been emotional but instead played out with unintentional comedy, bullets flying all around the characters.
Performance issues aside, Gears of War: E-Day's story and combat are both arguably the best the series has ever been, despite the pacing and structural drawbacks. Learning more about Marcus's and Dom's origins is fascinating, especially regarding the latter's concern for his family's whereabouts. Every new character introduced also has their place. (Shout-out to Mako and Manu, two Gears who happen to be Kiwi twins, and bring some of the best dialogue in series history as they riff off each other.)
E-Day is also built to be played in co-op. While your experience playing solo will be adequate, you'll have much more fun with a friend or three. The AI-led members of Bravo squad are nowhere near as competent as you need them to be on the tougher difficulty settings, and elite enemies will often make a beeline straight for you, ignoring your allies entirely.
Gears of War has languished for a long time. It's been seven years since the last mainline game Gears 5, and while it was a solid entry (there hasn't really been a disappointing Gears of War game, excluding spinoffs), it hasn't received the active, continuous support the series needs. It's not the only Xbox shooter to find itself in this position. Despite Halo: Campaign Evolved being well-received, a remake of a 25-year-old game isn't quite what Xbox's flagship IP deserves, either. Given the recent news that Halo is being absorbed by Activision, Gears of War: E-Day has an opportunity to step up and take the Xbox franchise crown from atop Master Chief's helmet. It's just about good enough to. Long live Marcus Fenix.
Gears of War: E-Day will be released Oct. 6 on Windows PC and Xbox Series X. The game was reviewed on PC using a prerelease download code provided by Xbox. The Horde Siege and multiplayer modes were not available during the review period. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

source_texts.text:
There are few blockbuster games that are as confident as Gears of War: E-Day. A prequel to one of Xbox’s most transformative titles, E-Day knows exactly what it wants to be: a brutal, tense, and self-aware action game, one that is stronger because it doesn’t deviate from that premise. Twenty years since the original Gears of War, there’s still nothing like its particular brand of up-close cover shooter gameplay, and E-Day shows that it still hits hard two decades later. As Xbox moves into a messy new era focused on its biggest franchises, E-Day could be an early glimpse at the future of the platform. But it’s also launching during one of the most tumultuous periods in Xbox history.
Gears of War: E-Day is a great game launching at a terrible time
A confident return for one of Xbox’s most iconic franchises is coming during a period of dramatic upheaval.
Gears of War: E-Day is a great game launching at a terrible time
A confident return for one of Xbox’s most iconic franchises is coming during a period of dramatic upheaval.
Set 14 years before the original Gears, E-Day tells the story of a pivotal point in the franchise’s sci-fi lore: “emergence day,” the moment when an alien collective known as the Locust Horde revealed itself with a surprise attack designed to wipe out the entire human race. You play as a slightly younger, but still gruff and experienced, soldier named Marcus Fenix as he and his squad attempt to fight back against the subterranean extraterrestrials. Marcus is part of an elite group known as “gears,” which are basically really buff guys and gals that wear massive armor and are thrown into action when things get really bad.
Things don’t get much worse than the events of E-Day. The human planet Sera is absolutely annihilated by the horde, which launches attacks from holes in the ground and has carved out a labyrinth of underground tunnels that allow them to strike anywhere. Marcus and his squad are thrown into the fray, tasked with doing everything they can to fight back and help where they’re able. Missions have you attacking enemy strongholds, escorting important supply caravans, and searching for survivors amid the rubble. Over the course of the game you see the planet turn from a retrofuturistic paradise to the ruins of a lost civilization.
E-Day is reminiscent of a James Cameron film: Absolutely every element is in service to creating a thrilling sci-fi spectacle. It’s as close to a playable Aliens as you’re bound to find. The cover shooter action remains visceral; everything has a weight to it, from Marcus’ slow movements to the chunky feel of reloading a shotgun. E-Day nails the sense of being pinned down in the middle of a war, surrounded on all sides, being terrified you’ll run out of bullets before the enemy does. There’s an unparalleled sense of tension.
E-Day does an excellent job of mixing things up so that you aren’t spending the whole game hiding behind chunks of concrete or burned-out husks of cars. There are huge set-pieces where the world crumbles around you as gigantic aliens lay waste to the city, and eerily quiet moments where you wander through a dark tunnel or foggy cemetery, unsure of what terrors await. E-Day has some side missions, but its world is largely linear, pushing you through one sequence after another with pacing that never really lets up. It’s all rendered with a lavish attention to detail on everything from the way blood splatters on the camera after a particularly gruesome kill to the outline of a leather wallet in the back pocket of Marcus’ jeans as he’s forced into combat in civilian clothes.
This conceit also means that, much like Avatar and its sequels, E-Day’s story is to the point and straightforward. Cutscenes give you just enough detail to care about the characters when dramatic things happen, but don’t get in the way of the action. No, the series hasn’t reached the emotion promised by the memorable “Mad World” commercial, but it doesn’t need to. In fact, much of the writing feels intentionally stupid, driving home that this is, at its very core, a dumb action game. The amount of ridiculous one-liners in the game approaches an art form, with pivotal moments punctuated by lines like “A giant floating ballsack with glowing eyes is trying to kill us!” or “Hold on to your dicks!” The true spiritual energy of E-Day can be found in its barks, those lines tossed out by Marcus and his comrades as they mow down alien bad guys. Here are a few examples:
- “Too ugly to live.”
- “Where are you going? I thought you wanted some of this.”
- “Rest in pieces.”
- “It ain’t your day, asshole.”
- “Looks dead to me.”
- “Lights out, fuckface.”
- “How do you like that, you stupid-ass spider bitch?”
That’s just a sampling. There’s a strangely joyous nature to the dialogue. The game is violent, the story is dire, but you’re still meant to enjoy the action of firing big guns and using a chainsaw to cut aliens in half. It feels good to play, and the campaign puts you through a range of emotions — at points it even approaches horror, with pitch-black tunnels teeming with bloodthirsty creatures — while never letting go of its action core. E-Day is a 2006 version of Gears rendered with the technology of 2026, which I mean as a total compliment: It’s a pure action game that isn’t saddled by modern trends.
It is also launching at an especially challenging time. Xbox is in the midst of “reset,” in which new CEO Asha Sharma is gutting the division, slashing around 3,200 jobs, and dramatically shaping how its current studios operate, with the ultimate — and perhaps unattainable — goal of focusing entirely on Xbox’s biggest franchises to reach a billion players. In a certain light, E-Day is indicative of this new approach, even if it predates Sharma’s time in charge. After launching tentpole franchises like Forza and Halo on the PlayStation 5, E-Day appears to represent a shift back to Xbox console exclusives. In essence, it’s a big, boisterous return for an iconic series, one that you can only play on Microsoft platforms. If you wanted an idea of what the future of Xbox could look like, E-Day offers an enticing vision.
I’m not entirely confident that the future will play out like that. Xbox’s strategic plans shift constantly, and E-Day developer The Coalition was hit with at least one layoff before launch, and staff fear more are coming. Xbox’s new leadership says that it wants to “focus on higher priority projects,” which on the surface sounds a lot like a bold, confident return for Gears of War. That’s exactly what you get with E-Day, but it might not be enough for whatever comes next for Xbox.
Gears of War: E-Day launches on October 6th on the PC and Xbox.

source_texts.summary: It's been over seven years since Vancouver-based studio The Coalition released its last game, Gears 5. According to a 2023 rumor by Jeff Grubb, that's because the developers canceled two unannounced side projects before focusing on Gears of War: E-Day. That's a long time for any studio, and especially so for one owned and funded by Xbox, which chose it to shepherd the Gears franchise after the split with Epic Games and is now also positioning it as a rare Xbox console exclusive. So far, The Coalition has done fairly well, or at least better than 343 Industries with Halo. […]
